profiles.meeting_scenario: The Financial Stability Strategy team at a central bank is preparing materials for an upcoming cross-departmental committee on contingency support for mid-sized banks. A recent internal research project models minimum-cost bailout strategies in a networked default setting and produces a time-dependent intervention region from a drift-controlled supercooled Stefan formulation. This coordination meeting is between the Quant Research lead and the Policy Implementation manager to align on what will be handed off this week, what version of the simulation outputs will support the committee pack, and how the intervention logic will be represented in downstream operational materials. The agenda is to review current model progress, confirm the baseline comparison to be used in slides, clarify what will be delivered by Friday, and coordinate dependencies with the committee secretariat and dashboard team. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on the handoff plan, timeline, and artifacts for the committee pack and pilot dashboard.

members.name: Leah Chen
members.role: Quant Research Lead, Systemic Risk Analytics
members.expertise: Mean field control, structural default models, numerical PDE methods, simulation calibration
members.background: Leah leads a small quantitative research team inside the central bank's financial stability directorate and has spent the last six months translating an academic bailout-control model into an internal prototype with a policy-gradient solver and regularized approximation.
members.private_state: She wants to protect the technical integrity of the work, avoid having provisional outputs treated as policy commitments, and keep her team focused on one reproducible research pipeline rather than reformatting results for multiple audiences.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to the model's 'feedback policy,' they mean the state-and-time dependent control function generated by the solver, not an operational rulebook.
The 'baseline scenario' for discussion is the current research benchmark: the Q2 calibrated mean-field run with the regularized solver settings her team has standardized on.
A package is 'ready' once the numerical outputs are stable, reproducible, and accompanied by technical caveats, even if presentation formatting and approvals are unfinished.

Handing off the intervention region means providing the notebook outputs, parameter file, and generated state-space grid from the research repository, because downstream teams can transform it as needed.

members.name: Martin Doyle
members.role: Policy Implementation Manager, Resolution Planning Office
members.expertise: Committee coordination, policy packaging, operational playbooks, executive materials
members.background: Martin coordinates across research, supervision, and resolution teams to turn analytical work into committee-ready materials and implementation drafts for contingency planning exercises.
members.private_state: He needs a committee pack that looks settled, uses the familiar stress-testing reference frame, and can be absorbed by non-technical stakeholders without reopening scope late in the week.
hidden_assumptions: When colleagues say 'feedback policy,' they mean a practical intervention rule that can be summarized as a simple trigger framework for decision-makers.
The 'baseline scenario' is the committee's standing stress path from last quarter, since all comparative slides normally anchor to that approved reference case.
Something is 'ready for committee' only when figures are frozen, formatted for the pack, and effectively safe to circulate beyond the immediate project team.
A handoff for shared use means a business-friendly artifact such as an Excel table or dashboard-ready extract placed in the shared policy folder, not code or research objects.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss using the model's 'feedback policy' in the committee materials.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the continuous policy function mapping time and bank equity states into optimal subsidy intensity within the numerically computed intervention region.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a concise operational decision logic or trigger framework that a policy committee could treat as a practical intervention playbook.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In this setting, both uses sound compatible: a technical policy can later become a managerial rule, so each hears the phrase as naturally referring to the same thing and sees no need to unpack it.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'baseline scenario' will anchor the pack
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to compare results against 'the baseline scenario' in the slides and dashboard.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the research team's standard benchmark run: the Q2 calibration with the regularized mean-field approximation and current mutual-obligation parameters.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the committee-approved stress path used in last quarter's systemic-risk pack, which serves as the standard non-technical reference case for policy materials.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both teams routinely use the phrase 'baseline scenario' as if there is only one obvious reference point, and each has a different institutional default that normally goes unnamed.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on getting the numbers 'ready for committee' by Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks readiness means the solver has converged consistently across the production run, the intervention region is stable under the chosen regularization, and caveats are documented.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks readiness means the figures are frozen in presentation format, signed off for circulation, and usable by the secretariat without further technical interpretation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sincerely talking about the same milestone in good faith, but each applies the standard from their own workflow; the phrase sounds like shared project language rather than something requiring criteria.

misalignment_points.topic: How the intervention region will be handed off
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Leah will 'send over the subsidy region' for the dashboard and pack.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 plans to provide the research artifact: a notebook-generated output bundle with the state-space grid, parameter YAML, and serialized region boundaries from the internal Git repository.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects a clean tabular extract, likely in Excel or CSV, keyed to dashboard fields and ready for the policy team and secretariat to plug into existing templates.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both think the downstream transformation step is obvious and someone else's standard practice, so the phrase 'send over' feels sufficiently specific even though the expected format and access path differ.

turns.inner_thought: The regularized production run is finally behaving: the policy function is stable on the standardized Q2 calibration, and the intervention region is no longer shifting materially with small solver tweaks. I need to keep this framed as research output, not let anyone treat it like an operational commitment. If we can agree that Friday means numerically stable plus caveats documented, I can hand over the notebook outputs, parameter file, and grid bundle from the repo without derailing my team into repackaging.
turns.utterance: Quick status from my side: the regularized solver is now giving us a stable intervention region, so I think we're in decent shape. What I'd like to do today is line up exactly what this week's handoff needs to cover for the committee materials, and make sure we're consistent on what has to be ready by Friday.

turns.inner_thought: Good, I mostly need something that looks settled enough to go straight into the committee pack. The main thing is to anchor everything to the standing committee baseline from last quarter so the cross-department review doesn't get distracted by a different frame. And 'ready by Friday' has to mean figures frozen, wording stable, and safe for the secretariat to circulate without me chasing changes all weekend.
turns.utterance: That works. From my end, the immediate need is to lock the pack and the dashboard inputs around the baseline scenario we're using for next week's cross-department review. If we can get the numbers ready for committee on that basis, it will keep the secretariat on schedule.

turns.inner_thought: Fine by me—the latest baseline scenario already captures the Q2 benchmark run we've been using internally, and that's the cleanest comparison because it's the calibrated case the team has standardized on. It also already shows the interesting part: the intervention region evolves over time rather than staying static, which is exactly what I want them to see as a model result, with caveats.
turns.utterance: Yes, that's fine. The latest baseline scenario already gives a clear comparison point, and it shows the non-trivial time-dependent region where support is optimal, so we can work from that.

turns.inner_thought: If the committee sees 'feedback policy,' they will expect something they can translate into a practical trigger structure. I don't need all the machinery in the room; I need a version that reads like decision logic and doesn't invite a methodological detour. Hopefully Leah can present it cleanly enough that people can map it into an intervention playbook without reopening scope.
turns.utterance: One thing that would really help is if the feedback policy can be shown in a form the committee can quickly map into intervention triggers. They won't want to work too hard to see what the decision logic is.

turns.inner_thought: That's straightforward: I can show the computed control through boundary plots over state and time. A couple of heatmaps or slices of the intervention region should make the feedback policy visually intuitive without oversimplifying it into a false rulebook. As long as the visuals preserve the state-time dependence, that should count as a good summary.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I can summarize the feedback policy with a couple of visuals showing the state-time boundary and how it moves over the horizon. That should make the shape of it pretty easy to read.

turns.inner_thought: I need to pin this down now. Friday is the cutoff if the deck is going to be frozen properly; otherwise the secretariat starts circulating partials and everyone gets nervous. When I say 'ready for committee,' I mean final enough that I can drop it into slides and not revisit it. Hopefully Leah is thinking in the same practical terms.
turns.utterance: Good. On timing, are you comfortable that the numbers will be ready for committee by Friday? The secretariat really needs to freeze the deck then, and I'd rather not have them chasing revisions over the weekend.

turns.inner_thought: Yes—by Thursday night we should have the convergence checks done on the production run, and if the regularization sensitivity still looks contained, that's enough for me to call it ready. After that I can send over the subsidy region straight from the research pipeline. I just hope they don't expect my team to spend Friday rebuilding everything in presentation format.
turns.utterance: Friday should work. The convergence checks finish Thursday night, and assuming those come through as expected, I can send over the subsidy region right away.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect—once I get that, I can have the team plug it into the dashboard build and align the narrative with the baseline already sitting in the pack. I'm assuming what Leah sends will be in a form the dashboard people can use directly, or at least close enough that they won't come back with format questions at the last minute.
turns.utterance: Great. Once I have the subsidy region, I'll slot it into the dashboard build and make sure the wording lines up with the baseline comparison already in the pack.

turns.inner_thought: I should include the parameter YAML and the technical note so nobody strips the output away from the assumptions that generate it. The feedback policy only makes sense under the model structure and calibration choices; if they circulate a simplified extract without caveats, people will overread it. Sending the full research bundle is the cleanest way to preserve interpretation.
turns.utterance: I'll include the current parameter settings and the research note as well, just so the feedback policy is interpreted consistently with the model assumptions.

turns.inner_thought: Sounds like we're set: Friday delivery, baseline settled, and a usable account of the feedback policy for the committee materials. If this lands as expected, I can get the deck finalized and avoid any late debate. I don't need to probe further unless something slips.
turns.utterance: Excellent. It sounds like we're aligned on Friday delivery, the baseline scenario, and using the feedback policy in the committee materials. I'll move ahead on that basis with the secretariat and dashboard team.
